newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Pan Pac plans to cut pulp production.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Pan Pac plans to cut pulp production.

text.p: Japanese-owned Pan Pacific Forest Industries (NZ) Ltd's (PanPac) said on Thursday it expects to supply around 220,000 tonnes in the 1997/98 year, against 240,000 tonnes in the March 1997 year.
Managing director Stuart McKinlay said the market was not strong globally at the moment, the New Zealand Press Association reported.
"There is an over supply of pulp," he said.
Long-term, the company, jointly owned by Oji Paper and Nippon Paper, hoped there would be a growing demand for radiata pulp despite competition with other wood species.
"I believe that 220,000 tonnes is stable and well assured," McKinlay said.

"The exchange rate movements in recent times are adversely affecting us and our cost of production as seen from the Japanese yen perspective has probably been an increase of about 30 percent in the last 12 months," McKinlay said.
"While exchange rate movements make Japanese cars cheaper for New Zealand buyers, it makes our product more expensive in Japan and that's not good for us or anyone exporting to that country."
The pulp mill capacity was expanded at the beginning of last year lifting potential annual production to 240,000 tonnes.

The company's Whirinaki sawmill on the east coast of the North Island is about halfway through a NZ$50 million expansion programme due for completion at the end of the year, which, McKinlay said, would make Pan Pac more competitive internationally.
The expansion would double sawmill production from 100,000cu metres a year to 200,000cu m, without any increase in staff.
"We don't see any reduction in staff but we don't see any increase either," McKinlay said. But there would be more jobs in the services industries supplying Pan Pac.

The Pan Pac mill produces pulp for exclusive use in Japan and the sawmill produces mainly for Japan, with some product going to the New Zealand market, Australia, a growing North American market and small quantities into South East Asia. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
